Neonatal Bonnethead sharks (Sphyrna tiburo) emerge from their mothers following a gestation period that culminates in live birth, with pups measuring approximately 31.5 cm [Lb = approximately 31.5 cm] in total length at birth. This size at parturition is consistent with the species’ modest adult dimensions compared to larger carcharhiniform sharks, and field surveys have documented a typical range of 30 to 33 cm (30-33 cm) [Lb = 30-33 cm] across populations in the Gulf of Mexico. The developing intrauterine embryo relies on a placental connection, absorbing nutrients through a yolk-sac placenta that supports organogenesis in utero until the foetal stage concludes. After exiting the maternal reproductive tract, the exotrophic transition begins as the pup commences independent foraging onset, targeting small crustaceans and cephalopods in shallow seagrass habitats. The age at birth has been determined from captive rearing studies conducted at a controlled water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], where the gestation period lasted approximately 145 days [ab = approximately 145 days], a duration that aligns with field observations of pregnant females collected in Florida Bay.

As the juvenile shark grows, it undergoes a period of rapid mass increase during its first few years, feeding intensively on blue crabs and penaeid shrimp to fuel somatic development. Sub-adult individuals begin to show the distinctive cephalofoil shape that characterizes the genus, and growth curves derived from tag-recapture data indicate that females achieve a substantially larger ultimate body size than males. The maximum recorded total length for adult females reaches 150 cm [Li = 150 cm], a value that places S. tiburo among the smaller hammerhead species but still within the typical dimensions of coastal carcharhiniforms. At this asymptotic length, the ultimate wet weight for females has been estimated at 11,140 grams [Wwi = 11,140 grams], a mass that reflects the robust body condition maintained by mature sharks foraging in productive estuarine systems. This adult body mass is achieved only after several years of sustained feeding and growth, with females continuing to add length and mass well beyond the onset of reproductive activity. The weight-length relationship for this species follows a typical elasmobranch allometric curve, with large gravid individuals representing the upper end of the size spectrum.

Sexual maturation in male Bonnethead sharks occurs at a smaller body size relative to females, a pattern common among many viviparous elasmobranchs where males invest less in somatic growth. Clasper-mediated fertilisation becomes possible once the male reaches puberty, which is attained at a total length of 61 cm [Lp = 61 cm], based on examination of clasper calcification and gonad maturation in specimens from the eastern Gulf of Mexico. At this pubertal size, the testicular recrudescence has begun, and spermatozoa are produced during the spring breeding season when water temperatures approach 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The onset of reproductive activity in males coincides with an increase in aggressive courtship behaviors, including biting of the female’s pectoral fins during copulation. Females, by contrast, delay their first pupping event until they have reached a larger body size, achieving reproductive maturity at 81 cm [Lp = 81 cm] total length. This size-at-maturity for females reflects the greater energetic demands of gestation and the need for a spacious abdominal cavity to accommodate developing embryos.

Reproductive output in this species is constrained by a single annual litter, with the maximum reproductive rate reflecting the gestation length and the number of pups produced per event. Under thermal conditions typical of the Gulf of Mexico in summer, approximately 25 °C [T = 25 °C], females produce litters ranging from 6 to 9 pups [N_R_i = litters ranging from 6 to 9 pups] per parturition. These litters are born after a gestation period of roughly 4.5 to 5 months, and the annual frequency is limited to one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year] due to the extended period required for yolk-sac resorption and follicular development prior to the next mating season. The combination of moderate litter size and single annual reproductive event means that each female typically contributes between 6 and 9 offspring [N_R_i = each female typically contributes between 6 and 9 offspring] each year, a rate that is typical for small coastal sharks with matrotroph embryo nourishment. Litter size can vary with maternal body condition and foraging success, with larger, more experienced females tending to produce the upper end of the range.

Longevity data for Bonnethead sharks, derived from mark-recapture studies and captive maintenance records, indicate that individuals have a maximum lifespan of approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years] when held at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. In the wild, natural mortality from predation by larger sharks and dolphins likely truncates this value for many individuals, but the species exhibits the characteristic elasmobranch life-history strategy of relatively slow growth, late maturity, and extended adult lifespan. The post-pubertal adult stage can last for several years, during which females may produce up to ten litters over their lifetime. Somatic death from senescence has been observed in captive animals after the twelfth year, with progressive deterioration of organ function marking the final stages of the species’ life cycle. This lifespan places S. tiburo in an intermediate position among its carcharhiniform relatives: longer than that of small bonnetheads in isolated estuaries with high predation pressure, but shorter than that of large, slow-maturing species in the same family such as the tiger shark. The combination of a 12-year maximum longevity (12 years) [am = 12 years] with a single annual reproductive event means that population recovery from overfishing is slow, requiring careful management of coastal fisheries where this species is commonly taken as bycatch at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].
